title: JUSTIFICATION FOR VIOLATION OF THE LAW
ops:
JUSTIFICATION FOR VIOLATION OF THE LAW
AND THE WATERGATE CONSPIRATORS\*
by
SAUL BRENNER
Assistant Professor
Department of Political Science
The University of North Carolina at Charlotte

The civil disobedience tradition of Henry David Thoreau and Mahatma Ghandi was rekindled in the 1950's by the direct action tactics of Martin Luther King and in the 1960's by the illegal activities of the anti-war movement. King was an authentic hero to almost all liberals and even won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964; while men such as Dr. Benjamin Spock, William Sloane Coffin, and Daniel Ellsberg achieved only a slightly lower status. To the people around Nixon, however, these men represented disrespect for the law, anarchy, and a threat to the American society. It is not surprising, therefore, that when the liberals accused the Watergate conspirators of violating the law, some of the accused retorted, "we were simply behaving like your heroes."
Jeb Stuart Magruder, testifying before the Ervin committee on June 14, 1973, presented this thesis in the following language:
During this whole time we were in the White House and during this time we were directly employed with trying to succeed with the President's policies we saw continuing violations of the law done by men like William Sloane Coffin. He tells me my ethics were bad. Yet he was indicted for criminal charges. He recommended on the Washington Monument grounds that students burn their draft cards and that we have mass demonstrations, shut down the city of Washington.
Now, here are ethical, legitimate people whom I respected. I respect Mr. Coffin tremendously. He was a very close friend of mine. I saw people I was very close to breaking the law without any regard for any other person's pattern of behavior or belief.
So consequently, when these subjects came up

To understand the complex moral landscape of the Watergate scandal, we must first look at the historical currents that shaped the political climate of the 1950s and 1960s. The tradition of civil disobedience—a deliberate, public, and non-violent violation of laws deemed unjust—was powerfully rekindled during this era. It was revitalized in the 1950s by the direct action tactics of Martin Luther King Jr. and further amplified in the 1960s by the illegal activities of the anti-war movement.

For the vast majority of liberals, figures like Martin Luther King were authentic heroes. King’s moral authority was so profound that he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. Other prominent figures, such as Dr. Benjamin Spock, William Sloane Coffin, and Daniel Ellsberg, occupied a similar, though perhaps slightly lower, tier of moral prestige in the public eye. However, the perspective from within the Nixon administration was starkly different. To the people surrounding President Nixon, these individuals did not represent moral courage; they represented a dangerous disrespect for the law, a slide toward anarchy, and a fundamental threat to the stability of American society.

This divergence in perspective sets the stage for a fascinating rhetorical defense used by the Watergate conspirators. When liberals accused the conspirators of violating the law, some of the accused retorted with a provocative counter-argument: "We were simply behaving like your heroes." This claim suggests that if breaking the law is acceptable when motivated by a "higher moral purpose" (as seen in the civil rights and anti-war movements), then the Watergate conspirators, who believed they were acting in the national interest, were operating under the same moral license.

Jeb Stuart Magruder, a key figure in the Watergate break-in, explicitly presented this thesis while testifying before the Ervin committee on June 14, 1973. His argument was not merely a legal defense but a moral comparison. He argued that during his time in the White House, while he was directly employed in trying to succeed with the President's policies, he witnessed continuing violations of the law by men like William Sloane Coffin. Magruder pointed out the hypocrisy he perceived: Coffin, who criticized Magruder’s ethics, had himself been indicted for criminal charges. Magruder recalled that Coffin had recommended, on the grounds of the Washington Monument, that students burn their draft cards and organize mass demonstrations that would shut down the city of Washington.

Magruder emphasized the personal nature of this conflict. He stated, "Now, here are ethical, legitimate people whom I respected. I respect Mr. Coffin tremendously. He was a very close friend of mine. I saw people I was very close to breaking the law without any regard for any other person's pattern of behavior or belief."

This personal connection was crucial to his argument. Magruder suggested that because he saw respected friends breaking the law for what they considered just causes, the moral barrier to breaking the law was eroded. He explained, "So consequently, when these subjects came up,
although I was aware they were
we had become somewhat inured to using some activities that would help us in accomplishing what we thought was a cause, a legitimate
(Staff of The New York Times, 1973, p. 258)

The term "inured" is significant here. It implies that through repeated exposure to the idea that law-breaking could be justified by higher moral ends, the conspirators became hardened or accustomed to the practice. The moral shock of breaking the law diminished over time, replaced by a sense of necessity.

This theme was not limited to Magruder.
On August 15, 1973, Richard Nixon, in a broadcast to the nation, voiced the same
that Watergate had its roots in the

"as individuals and groups increasingly asserted their right to take the law into their own hands, insisting that their purposes represented a higher morality." (Staff of The New York Times, 1973, p. 708)
By framing the scandal as a reaction to the permissiveness of the 1960s, Nixon
were not alone in comparing the activities of the Watergate conspirators with
their civil rights and anti-war opponents.
This comparison was echoed in mainstream media and academic circles.
In a CBS evening news program on May 2, 1973, Eric Sevareid offered the following commentary:

It may be worth pointing out that the Watergate operators obeyed the same kind of motivation as thousands of street rioters, including students. Both responded to what they conceived to be higher law, racial riots, or ending the war, or, in the minds of the Watergate crew, preventing the election of people they judged to be dangerous to the country in a dangerous world. (Sego 1973, p. 22)

Sevareid’s point highlights a critical philosophical concept: the appeal to "higher law." This is the idea that there are moral principles that supersede positive law (the laws written by the state). If a law violates these higher moral principles, some argue that individuals have a right, or even a duty, to disobey it.

Similarly,
The rationale offered by Daniel Ellsberg for taking and publishing government documents was the same as that offered by the Watergate conspirators -- national interest, a higher law ... (p. 30)

Wildavsky’s observation is particularly sharp because Daniel Ellsberg, the whistleblower who released the Pentagon Papers, is widely regarded as a hero by many who value transparency and democratic oversight. If Ellsberg’s theft of documents was justified by the "national interest" and "higher law," then the Watergate conspirators’ actions, which they also claimed were driven by the "national interest," might seem to share the same moral foundation.

This article examines whether the hypothesis suggested by these quotations can be supported. In other words, on what philosophical grounds, if any, can we distinguish between the justification for the violation of law offered by those in the civil rights and anti-war movements and those offered by the Watergate conspirators?
Are they truly morally equivalent, or is there a fundamental difference in their justifications?
Philosophical Grounds for Violation of Law

In discussing the general grounds upon which one might base a claim that violation of the law is justified, it is necessary to raise questions concerning the moral obligation to obey the law: (1) Does such an obligation exist? (2) If it does, on what principle does it rest? (3) Is the obligation absolute? which means that under any and all circumstances one is obliged to obey the law; or is it prima facie only? which means that there is a presumption in favor of obligation, but under certain circumstances this presumption can be set aside. (4) And if prima facie, what sort of considerations override it?
we must step back and examine the general philosophical grounds upon which one might base a claim that violation of the law is justified. This requires us to raise several fundamental questions

law. Anarchists and some utilitarians have denied the existence of such an obligation, while social contract theorists, idealists, and other utilitarians have affirmed it. It appears that the duty to obey the law ought to depend upon the legitimacy of the government that enacted the law. For implicit in the concept of the right of the government to enact laws is an acceptance of the duty to obey the laws of such a government. What confers legitimacy upon government? In modern society what is required is democracy, a political system in which every sane, noncriminal, adult citizen has the right to choose the major rulers of the society in periodic free elections. I would contend that all citizens of a democracy can be thought of as having tacitly consented to obey the law. Conversely, no obligation to obey the law exists if the political system is undemocratic. Some laws, however, ought to be followed even in the absence of such an obligation. One should not murder or steal even if one has no duty to obey the law because to do so would be immoral whether there are laws to that effect or not. But if the law in question is not of this kind and one has no duty to obey the law, one's illegal behavior needs no further justification.

Violation of a particular law can also be justified even if one has an obligation to obey the law in general, provided such an obligation is prima facie. Since there is no reason why the obligation to obey the law should always be given primacy over other conflicting moral obligations, the duty to obey the law ought to be considered prima facie only. Two general approaches have been employed by philosophers to determine whether, in a particular case, the circumstances warrant obedience to law. Some philosophers - part of either the divine law or the natural law tradition - have focused upon the substantive content of the law in question, comparing it with some higher law or principle derived from God, nature, reason or conscience. Others have used a utilitarian approach and have been concerned with the consequences surrounding the law, typically weighing the consequences of disobedience against the consequences of obedience. A utilitarian approach is employed in this article. In using this orientation, it will be assumed that a person who violates a law and seeks justification on the ground of conflicting moral duty has a responsibility to use the time and effort necessary to become aware of the foreseeable consequences of his action. (The situation described at this point is usually discussed using the term "civil disobedience." For an act to be "civil disobedience," as this term is usually defined by philosophers, there must be (1) a prima facie obligation to obey the law, (2) a violation of a specific law, (3) performed by reasons of conscience; and the act must be (4) an act of protest, (5) performed publicly. The term "civil disobedience" is not used since it appears to this writer that violation of the law can be justified though it does not involve public protest.)

1.  **Does such an obligation exist?** This is the foundational question. Do citizens have a moral duty to follow the laws of their country, or is obedience purely a matter of self-interest or fear of punishment?
2.  **If it does, on what principle does it rest?** If we do have an obligation to obey the law, why is that so? Is it because of a social contract we implicitly agreed to? Is it because the law is necessary for social order? Or is it because the law is inherently just?
3.  **Is the obligation absolute?** This means that under any and all circumstances, one is obliged to obey the law. If the obligation is absolute, then no amount of moral outrage or perceived injustice can justify breaking the law.
4.  **Or is it *prima facie* only?** The term *prima facie* is a Latin phrase meaning "at first sight" or "on the face of it." In ethics, a *prima facie* obligation is a presumption in favor of an action, but one that can be overridden by other, stronger moral considerations. If the obligation to obey the law is *prima facie*, then there is a default expectation that we should follow the law, but under certain circumstances, this presumption can be set aside.
5.  **And if *prima facie*, what sort of considerations override it?** If we accept that the obligation to obey the law is not absolute, we must define the specific conditions under which it is permissible to break the law. Is it only when the law is grossly unjust? Only when there is no other way to achieve a significant moral good? Only when the harm caused by breaking the law is less than the harm caused by obeying it?

These questions form the philosophical framework within which we must evaluate the actions of both the civil rights activists and the Watergate conspirators.

Philosophers have long debated a fundamental question: Do we have a moral obligation to obey the law? This is not a trivial inquiry; it strikes at the heart of political philosophy and ethics. The academic landscape is divided into two main camps. On one side, anarchists and certain utilitarians argue that no such inherent obligation exists. On the other side, social contract theorists, idealists, and other utilitarians affirm that we do have a duty to comply with legal statutes.

To navigate this conflict, we must look for a common ground. It appears that the duty to obey the law is not absolute but rather conditional. It depends heavily on the **legitimacy** of the government that enacted the law. Think of it this way: the very concept of a government having the *right* to make laws is paired with the *duty* of citizens to obey them. If the government lacks the right (legitimacy), the corresponding duty to obey evaporates.

So, what confers legitimacy upon a government? In modern society, the standard is **democracy**. Democracy is a political system defined by specific criteria: every sane, non-criminal, adult citizen must have the right to choose the major rulers of the society through periodic, free elections.

Based on this framework, we can draw a strong conclusion: All citizens of a democracy can be thought of as having **tacitly consented** to obey the law. Tacit consent means that by living in and benefiting from a democratic system, you have implicitly agreed to its rules, even if you never signed a formal contract. Conversely, if the political system is undemocratic (a dictatorship, for example), this specific obligation to obey the law does not exist.

However, a crucial nuance remains. Even in an undemocratic system where there is no general duty to obey the law, some actions are still morally forbidden. For instance, one should not murder or steal, even if one has no legal duty to obey the law. Why? Because these acts are inherently immoral, independent of whether a statute prohibits them. Morality exists prior to and separate from legislation. But, if a law is not of this "inherently immoral" kind (like murder) and you have no general duty to obey the law, then your illegal behavior requires no further justification. You are simply acting according to your own moral compass, free from the constraint of state authority.

Now, let us return to the democratic context where an obligation to obey the law *does* exist. Can this obligation ever be broken? Yes. Violation of a particular law can be justified even if one has a general obligation to obey the law, provided that this obligation is **prima facie**.

*   **Mentor’s Note:** The term *prima facie* (Latin for "at first sight") is critical here. It means that the obligation is valid and binding *unless* it is outweighed by a stronger, conflicting moral duty. It is not an absolute, unbreakable rule.

Since there is no logical reason why the obligation to obey the law should always take priority over other moral duties (such as the duty to prevent harm or to uphold justice), the duty to obey the law must be considered *prima facie* only. It is a strong default, but not an invincible one.

How do we determine, in a specific case, whether the circumstances warrant obedience or disobedience? Philosophers have generally employed two approaches:

1.  **The Natural/Divine Law Approach:** Some philosophers, often from the divine law or natural law traditions, focus on the **substantive content** of the law. They compare the specific law in question against a "higher law" or principle derived from God, nature, reason, or conscience. If the human law contradicts this higher moral truth, it may be justified to disobey.
2.  **The Utilitarian Approach:** Others use a utilitarian framework. This approach is concerned with **consequences**. It typically involves weighing the negative consequences of disobedience against the positive (or less negative) consequences of obedience. The goal is to maximize overall well-being or minimize harm.

This article adopts the **utilitarian approach**. When using this orientation, we make a specific assumption: A person who violates a law and seeks justification on the ground of a conflicting moral duty has a **responsibility** to use the time and effort necessary to become aware of the foreseeable consequences of their action. You cannot claim to be acting for the greater good if you have not diligently investigated what that action will actually cause.

*(The situation described at this point is usually discussed using the term "civil disobedience." For an act to be "civil disobedience," as this term is usually defined by philosophers, there must be: (1) a prima facie obligation to obey the law, (2) a violation of a specific law, (3) performed by reasons of conscience; and the act must be (4) an act of protest, (5) performed publicly. The term "civil disobedience" is not used here since it appears to this writer that violation of the law can be justified though it does not involve public protest.)*

Up to now, it has been assumed that what constitutes "the law" in a particular case was not in dispute. But often, this assumption is incorrect. Does the obligation to obey the law imply a duty to obey a particular rule if one believes it is contrary to a constitution or some other legal standard? The philosopher Ronald Dworkin has suggested three possible answers to this question: (1) one ought to defer to the law as the

police or other executive officials who enforce it are likely to define it: (2) one ought to defer to the law as the courts are likely to define it; (3) if one's argument is reasonable, one may follow one's own view of the law "even after a contrary decision by the highest competent court." (Murphy,1971, p. 117) Dworkin favors the third position.

understand the weight of these options, let us pause and examine the underlying logic. We are looking at three distinct ways a citizen might relate to the legal system when they believe a law is unjust. The first option suggests we should look to the police or the executive branch (the people enforcing the law) to tell us what the law means. The second option suggests we should look to the courts (the judges) to tell us what the law means. The third option, favored by the legal philosopher Ronald Dworkin, suggests that if a citizen has a reasonable moral argument, they are permitted to follow their own interpretation of the law, even if the highest court has ruled against them.

Now, it appears that the duty to obey the law implies a deference to the courts' definition of the law. For, in modern societies, it is the courts that have the final authority to decide questions of legality. Therefore, this writer favors the second position in the above and would argue that if it is more probable than not that a rule of doubtful legality will be upheld by the highest court that is likely to hear the case, then, one has a duty to obey that rule. If the converse is the case, then no such duty exists. If the issue of illegality is unlikely to be considered by the courts because of the doctrine of "political question" or for any other reason, that determination is an acquiescence to the decision of executive officials and a decision against the claim of illegality.

Let’s unpack this argument, as it contains the core mechanism for deciding when civil disobedience is justified. The author is adopting a **probabilistic approach** to legal obligation. Instead of asking, "Is this law morally good?" the author asks, "What is the likelihood that the highest court will strike this law down?"

Here is the strategic logic:

1.  **The Court as the Ultimate Arbiter:** In a modern democracy, the courts are the final word on what the law *actually* is. Therefore, your obligation to obey the law is tied to the court's likely interpretation.
2.  **The "More Probable Than Not" Threshold:** If there is a greater than 50% chance that the highest court will rule a specific rule is illegal or unconstitutional, then you do **not** have a duty to obey it. Conversely, if the court is likely to uphold the rule, you **do** have a duty to obey it.
3.  **The "Political Question" Trap:** What happens if the courts refuse to hear the case? Sometimes, courts declare an issue a "political question," meaning it is not for the judiciary to decide but for the political branches (executive/legislative). The author argues that if the courts step aside, this silence effectively validates the executive branch's enforcement of the law. In other words, if the courts won't rule the law illegal, the law stands, and the duty to obey remains.

One is now ready for the difficult task of attempting to apply this theoretical structure to determine whether the illegal activities of the civil rights movement, the anti-war movement, and the Watergate conspirators can be justified.

In discussing the civil rights violations, for this paper, the focus is exclusively upon the non-violent, direct action phase, rather than upon the later "black militant" phase, though both involved violations of the law. The sit-ins, demonstrations and other violations of the law which were part of the non-violent, direct action phase of the civil rights movement of the late 1950's and early 1960's were conducted in opposition to public accommodation and other discriminatory state laws and local ordinances. These violations of law can be justified on several grounds:

(1) The civil rights activists did not have an obligation to obey the state law in general since it was a product of an undemocratic political system by virtue of the states' denial of the right of the blacks to vote.

(2) These activists did not have an obligation to obey the specific laws involved because, as they claimed, there was a greater probability than not that the highest courts that would hear their cases would hold these laws to be in conflict with the United States Constitution or some other legal standard. (Of the 81 sit-in cases that came before the Supreme Court during the 1957 to 1967 period, 61 were granted review, of which 57 were decided in favor of the demonstrators [Grossman and Tanenhaus, 1969, p. 427]).
(3) Even if these demonstrators had a duty to obey the law in general and a duty to obey the specific laws involved, the consequences of
disobedience were morally preferable to those

of obedience since their actions helped destroy the immoral segregation system and furthered the entry of blacks into the mainstream of American life. It is true that their actions also may have encouraged violations of law under circumstances less moral than those under which they were acting, but this possible adverse consequence clearly is outweighed by the impressive positive ones.

The Anti-War Violations
Within the anti-war movement of the 1960's were people of differing moral commitments who employed a great variety of strategies and tactics in their effort to end American military involvement in Vietnam. Many of these activities were legal. Those that were not ranged from peaceful marches without a permit to the bombing of draft boards and ROTC buildings. Some of these illegal activities can be justified and others cannot be. For purposes of this article, a situation is focused upon which in recent years has interested many philosophers concerned with justification for violation of law. The situation involves men who have been turned down by the courts in their efforts to obtain a conscientious objector classification, have been ordered for induction, and refuse to serve, claiming that one ought not to participate in an unjust war. The philosopher Robert Booth Fowler has argued that most men of draft age did not have an obligation to obey the law since they did not have a meaningful opportunity to participate in the American political system (Hanson and Fowler, 1971, p. 54). That is, at the time of the anti-war protest eighteen-year-olds did not have the right to vote. It appears that the crucial criterion for obligation to obey the law is not the right to participate as such but the (democratic) nature of the political system. To argue otherwise would also imply that younger children, criminals, the insane and aliens have no obligation to obey the law in a democratic country since they have no right to participate. This writer contends that a political system has the right to select an age when citizens are granted political rights and that the age of twenty-one is a reasonable one (though this writer happens to prefer the subsequently enacted eighteen) and that its use does not render the system undemocratic. Therefore, if a justification for this type of illegal activity can be urged persuasively, it must be based upon a claim that there is a stronger moral obligation to violate the draft law than to obey it. Such a claim is justifiable. In so arguing, it is assumed that the American involvement in Vietnam was an involvement in an unjust war. This war was unjust because it supported an illegitimate, authoritarian and, at times, cruel government. Admittedly, American participation may have prevented the immediate North Vietnamese or Viet Cong takeover of South Vietnam, but such takeover was likely to occur anyway as soon as the Americans left. To enable the South Vietnamese people to live under their former bad government for a period of time instead of the bad government of the North Vietnamese or Viet Cong was hardly worth the human suffering which resulted from the American participation in the war. Moreover, our use of such vast quantities of men and material in this war may have hampered our efforts in preventing communist penetration in more strategic areas of the world.

### The Anti-War Violations

Within the anti-war movement of the 1960's were people of differing moral commitments who employed a great variety of strategies and tactics in their effort to end American military involvement in Vietnam. Many of these activities were legal. Those that were not ranged from peaceful marches without a permit to the bombing of draft boards and ROTC buildings. Some of these illegal activities can be justified and others cannot be. For purposes of this article, a situation is focused upon which in recent years has interested many philosophers concerned with justification for violation of law. The situation involves men who have been turned down by the courts in their efforts to obtain a conscientious objector classification, have been ordered for induction, and refuse to serve, claiming that one ought not to participate in an unjust war.

To understand the complexity of this refusal, we must first look at the legal and political landscape of the time. The philosopher Robert Booth Fowler has argued that most men of draft age did not have an obligation to obey the law since they did not have a meaningful opportunity to participate in the American political system (Hanson and Fowler, 1971, p. 54). That is, at the time of the anti-war protest eighteen-year-olds did not have the right to vote.

Here, we encounter a critical logical pivot point. One might initially think: "If I cannot vote for the leaders who are sending me to war, I have no stake in the system, and therefore, I have no duty to obey its laws." This is Fowler’s argument. However, we must pause and examine the implications of this line of reasoning. If we accept that the *right to vote* is the sole criterion for the *obligation to obey the law*, we run into significant logical problems. To argue otherwise would also imply that younger children, criminals, the insane and aliens have no obligation to obey the law in a democratic country since they have no right to participate.

Think about this: Do we really believe that a ten-year-old child has no obligation to stop at a red light? Or that a criminal has no obligation to follow traffic laws while fleeing? Clearly, the obligation to obey basic laws exists independently of one's voting status. Therefore, it appears that the crucial criterion for obligation to obey the law is not the right to participate as such but the (democratic) nature of the political system. In other words, the legitimacy of the state comes from its democratic structure, not from whether every individual citizen currently holds a ballot.

This writer contends that a political system has the right to select an age when citizens are granted political rights and that the age of twenty-one is a reasonable one (though this writer happens to prefer the subsequently enacted eighteen) and that its use does not render the system undemocratic. Therefore, if a justification for this type of illegal activity can be urged persuasively, it must be based upon a claim that there is a stronger moral obligation to violate the draft law than to obey it.

So, if the argument from "lack of voting rights" fails, how can the refusal to serve be justified? The answer lies in the content of the law itself, not the procedure of the state. Such a claim is justifiable. In so arguing, it is assumed that the American involvement in Vietnam was an involvement in an unjust war. This war was unjust because it supported an illegitimate, authoritarian and, at times, cruel government.

Admittedly, American participation may have prevented the immediate North Vietnamese or Viet Cong takeover of South Vietnam, but such takeover was likely to occur anyway as soon as the Americans left. To enable the South Vietnamese people to live under their former bad government for a period of time instead of the bad government of the North Vietnamese or Viet Cong was hardly worth the human suffering which resulted from the American participation in the war. Moreover, our use of such vast quantities of men and material in this war may have hampered our efforts in preventing communist penetration in more strategic areas of the world.

But the crucial question for us is not whether the war was justifiable, but whether refusing induction during this war was justifiable. It is necessary, therefore, to examine the consequences of the actions of these men.

In moral philosophy, we often evaluate the permissibility of civil disobedience not just by the intent of the actor, but by the tangible outcomes of their actions. Here, we must weigh the potential benefits against the potential harms.
It is maintained that their refusal enabled them to avoid participation in an unjust war and encouraged others to follow their example.

This argument rests on the idea of **moral signaling**. By refusing to serve, these individuals created a visible precedent, demonstrating that conscience could override legal obligation. This act of defiance served as a beacon, potentially inspiring others who shared similar moral reservations to also step out of line, thereby amplifying the collective voice of dissent.

In addition, their refusal may have fostered among political leaders a sensitivity to the immorality of this particular war or, at least, a sensitivity to the necessity of justifying war on credible moral grounds.

Think of this as a form of **political friction**. When a significant number of citizens refuse to comply, it forces the state to slow down and justify its actions more rigorously. It compels leaders to articulate clear, defensible moral reasons for their policies, rather than relying on vague appeals to patriotism or duty. This friction can be a healthy check on executive power, ensuring that the machinery of war does not operate without moral scrutiny.
On the other hand, it is possible to argue that those who refused induction may have made it more difficult for the United States to draft men for morally justifiable future wars.

This is the **precedent risk** argument. If the draft system is weakened by widespread refusal, the state might struggle to mobilize quickly in a future crisis where military action is genuinely necessary and just. However, the text notes a critical counterpoint:
in view of the popular opposition to amnesty for draft evaders, even for this war, this is unlikely.

The public’s strong desire to hold evaders accountable suggests that the legal framework for conscription remained robust enough to deter widespread evasion in future scenarios. Consequently, the fear that the draft system was permanently compromised by these specific acts of refusal is not well-supported by the social climate of the time.

Thus,
the arguments in favor of disobedience to the draft laws are stronger than those urging obedience.

The moral weight of avoiding participation in an unjust conflict, combined with the positive effect of forcing political accountability, outweighs the speculative risk to future military readiness.

###

To speak concerning the justification for violation of law of the Watergate conspirators is somewhat peculiar. For unlike the civil rights and anti-war activists, these men were at the very center of the federal government and, as such, were in a crucial position to change any law they deemed contrary to conscience.

we encounter a fundamental shift in the dynamics of civil disobedience. In previous cases, we considered individuals who were marginalized or powerless against the state. The Watergate conspirators, however, were the state. This distinction is vital. When a citizen breaks a law, they are often acting from a position of vulnerability, using their body or their freedom as the only leverage they have. When a government official breaks a law, they are acting from a position of immense power.

If the campaign laws were too restrictive they were in an excellent position to urge that position on Congress. If the "President's men" believed it necessary to wiretap or break in for reasons of national security, they also could have proposed legislation to that effect and maybe persuade Congress to enact it.

This highlights the **availability of legal channels**. The conspirators had direct access to the legislative process. They did not need to resort to illegal surveillance or burglary because they had the institutional tools to change the rules legally. The argument here is that when you hold the pen that writes the law, you cannot claim that the law is unjust and then simply ignore it; you have a duty to use your power to reform it.

The President himself had already selected four members of the United States Supreme Court, all of whom, we have reason to believe, might be sympathetic to upholding the constitutionality of campaign and national security legislation of this kind.

This point underscores the **institutional control** the administration held. They were not fighting against an entrenched, hostile judiciary that would inevitably strike down their desired policies. They had the ability to shape the legal landscape to their advantage through the appointment process. Therefore, the claim that they were forced to break the law because the legal system was blocked is factually weak.

Thus, when discussing justification here we are not confronted with a case of the weak violating a law for reasons of conscience and, by doing so, opposing the might of government; but, instead, we have a case of powerful government officials violating the law and using all the resources of their positions to protect themselves.

This inversion of the typical civil disobedience narrative is critical. Civil disobedience is traditionally a tool of the powerless to challenge the powerful. In Watergate, the powerful used illegal means to maintain their power. This is not resistance; it is corruption.
The philosopher Jeffrie G. Murphy has pointed out the crucial differences between the government's obligation to obey the law and of individual citizens. He wrote:

...this obligation falls most heavily upon the government itself. For if an individual citizen fails to obey the law, the damage he can do is minimal. We also have institutions to deal with him... But government is not in the position of the average citizen. Government holds a near monopoly on the force in a given society, and this makes it both highly dangerous and invulnerable. Thus its deviations from the rule of law present a threat to the integrity of society far beyond that posed by any individual citizen. Even more important, of course, is the fact that government ... has the solemn trust of preserving the rule of law. It must call upon its citizens for obedience; and if it is to be morally persuasive and not merely coercive in doing this, its own

hands must be clean.

The government holds a monopoly on legitimate force and the administration of law; therefore, its justification for breaking the law must be overwhelming.
Let us examine the possible conflicting moral obligations that were urged by the Watergate conspirators to determine whether they meet this burden.

One justification spoke of insuring the election of Richard Nixon. The dirty tricks, the campaign bribery and extortion money, and the Watergate break-in itself can be associated with this justification. A second spoke of national security. The burglary of Ellsberg's psychiatrist, the alleged attempt to influence the judge in the Ellsberg case, the attempt to get the Internal Revenue Bureau to audit the returns of those on an enemies list, the Watergate cover-up, and, again, the Watergate break-in can be associated with this second justification.
To evaluate them, we must ask three critical questions:
Were the actions of these men reasonably calculated to achieve their goals? What adverse consequences resulted from their activities?
And did the ends truly justify the means?

It is common knowledge that Richard Nixon was a heavy favorite to win the presidency in 1972 in view of both his domestic success in quieting the nation after the turbulence of the 1960's and his foreign success in China and in the Soviet Union. This was particularly so after the selection of George McGovern as the Democratic nominee. It is reasonable to conclude, therefore, that the Watergate conspirators could have reasonably foreseen that, rather than insuring the election of the President, their actions would only succeed in subverting the presidential election process.
In other words, the "means" (illegal surveillance and sabotage) were not only unnecessary but counterproductive to the stated "end" (winning the election).

Concerning national security, the only serious argument presented is that they were attempting to prevent leaks from the National Security Council. But no solid evidence has been produced which supports the contention that their activities were reasonably calculated to prevent such leaks. There is ample evidence, however, that their actions violated the civil liberties of a number of citizens. Moreover, the activities of the Watergate group, in both of these areas, probably contributed to a popular loss of confidence in the federal government. There were many other adverse consequences of the actions of the Watergate conspirators. But it is unnecessary to enumerate them. For even the cursory examination just presented makes it clear that the case for justification is exceedingly weak.

Indeed, it is ludicrous to compare their situation with that of the civil rights and anti-war activists. In the language of one recent observer, "we can lay to rest the theory that the real Watergate conspirators were Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King." (Steinfels, 1973, p. 470).
